draft.title: Choosing form and audience
card: Start with two questions. Who is this writing for, and what should it do to them? The answers come before any decision about form.
the people who will read or hear the piece. Their age, knowledge and values shape the tone, the language and the amount of explanation.
what the writer wants the piece to do, such as persuade, entertain, inform or reflect.

the shape that carries the purpose to the audience. A speech is heard live, so it suits repetition and direct address. An opinion piece argues a view. A short story shows an idea through characters and events. A personal essay explores the writer's own thinking.
draft.remember: Decide the audience and purpose first, then choose the form that best carries them.

a.q: Why should a writer decide the audience and purpose before choosing a form?
opts: The form should be the one that best suits them
Each form has only one audience that can read it
The form decides the purpose, so it must come first
Audience and purpose matter only for opinion pieces
a.why: Form is a tool for reaching a particular audience with a particular purpose, so those choices guide it. The third option reverses this: form does not decide the purpose.
a.clue: Is the form the goal, or the tool for reaching one?

b.q: Priya wants to persuade her school's students to join a beach clean-up. She will deliver it live at assembly. Which form suits her purpose and audience best?
opts: A speech with direct address and repeated phrases
A personal essay exploring her private memories
A short story about an invented character at sea
A report with long tables of data on rubbish
b.why: A live speech reaches the whole audience at once. Direct address and repetition help listeners follow and act. A personal essay explores the writer's own thinking, so it does not suit a call to act, even though it can be persuasive.
b.clue: Think about how the audience will receive it: listening, not reading.

a.best: The form should be the one that best suits them

b.best: A speech with direct address and repeated phrases
